Mixed endpoint Green kernel for a first-derivative drift (y′′+y′=f,y(0)=0, y′(1)=0)

Words: 67
Green's function OurBigBook.com
Multiplying the equation for v=y′ by the integrating factor ex gives v(x)=−e−x∫x1​etf(t)dt. Integrating once more and reversing the order of integration gives the Green's function
G(x,t)={1−et,et−x−et,​t≤x,x≤t.​
(1)
It is continuous across x=t, its first derivative has jump +1, and it satisfies the mixed Dirichlet boundary condition and Neumann boundary condition. Both homogeneous solutions, 1 and e−x, are eliminated by these two conditions, giving uniqueness. For f=e−x the solution is −xe−x.

GL​(x,s)=sinLsin(min{x,s})sin(L−max{x,s})​.
(2)

Adjoint Green function

Words: 75
Green's function OurBigBook.com
An adjoint Green's function solves the corresponding adjoint point-source problem, with boundary or terminal conditions chosen so that integration by parts gives a representation for a solution of the original operator. For L=∂t​−∂x2​+c on the real line, the formal adjoint is L∗=−∂t​−∂x2​+c. The backward kernel with terminal Dirac delta at (ξ,τ) is the translated heat kernel with constant absorption, defined for t<τ. Its pairing with a homogeneous forward solution is constant in t; taking the terminal limit evaluates that solution at (ξ,τ).

Green function jump conditions

Words: 56
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For L=a2​(x)D2+a1​(x)D+a0​(x) with a2​(ξ)=0, a Green's function solving Lx​G=δ(x−ξ) is homogeneous on either side of ξ, continuous there, and has first derivative jump [Gx​]−+​=1/a2​(ξ). A nonzero jump in G itself would produce an unwanted distributional derivative of the Dirac delta. Once continuity removes that term, integrating the equation across ξ fixes the derivative jump. Endpoint boundary conditions complete the classical characterization.

Green function under dependent-variable rescaling (L(qv)=rMv⟹GL​(x,s)=q(x)GM​(x,s)/r(s))

Words: 120
Green's function OurBigBook.com
Suppose a linear ordinary differential operator satisfies L(qv)=rMv on an interval, where the functions q,r never vanish and homogeneous endpoint boundary conditions for y=qv correspond to those used for v. If GM​ is a Green's function for M, then Ly=f is equivalent to Mv=f/r, so
y(x)=q(x)∫GM​(x,s)r(s)f(s)​ds.
(4)
Thus the displayed kernel is the Green's function for the original, possibly non-normalized operator. The source factor belongs at s, while the dependent-variable factor belongs at x.
For Ly=x2y′′−2xy′+(x2+2)y on [π/2,π] with zero endpoint values, q=x and r=x3 reduce the equation to Mv=v′′+v. The kernel of M is cos(x<​)sin(x>​), where x<​=min(x,s) and x>​=max(x,s). Therefore GL​(x,s)=xcos(x<​)sin(x>​)/s3. Its first derivative has jump 1/s2, as required by the leading coefficient s2 of L.

Mixed Dirichlet-Neumann Green function in a quadrant (G=4π1​log[(x−ξ)2+(y+η)2][(x+ξ)2+(y+η)2][(x−ξ)2+(y−η)2][(x+ξ)2+(y−η)2]​)

Words: 127
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For the quadrant x,y>0, the displayed Green function satisfies ΔG=δ(ξ,η)​, zero value on y=0 and zero outward normal derivative on x=0. The method of images uses the logarithmic fundamental solution of the Laplace equation with coefficient 1/(2π): keep the source sign when reflecting across the Neumann side and reverse it when reflecting across the Dirichlet side. The four image signs are therefore +,+,−,− for sources (ξ,η),(−ξ,η),(ξ,−η),(−ξ,−η).
On y=0, equal numerator and denominator give zero. Evenness in x gives the Neumann condition at x=0. The outward normal derivative on the Dirichlet side is the positive kernel
∂n​G(x,0,ξ,η)=πη​((x−ξ)2+η21​+(x+ξ)2+η21​).
(5)
Green's second identity consequently gives u(P)=∫D​Gf+∫y=0​g∂n​G for Δu=f with these mixed boundary data, assuming any remote-boundary contribution vanishes. The sign convention is ΔG=+δ; changing to −ΔG=δ changes both the Green function and the representation signs.

Boundary-matrix construction of an ordinary differential Green function (G=G0​−hTM−1b)

Words: 112
Green's function OurBigBook.com
Let h1​,…,hn​ be a basis of homogeneous solutions of a linear ordinary differential operator L of order n. Let B1​,…,Bn​ be independent homogeneous linear boundary conditions, which may be coupled. Suppose a fundamental solution G0​(x,ξ) satisfies Lx​G0​=δ(x−ξ). Define the boundary matrix Mij​=Bi​hj​ and bi​(ξ)=Bi​G0​(⋅,ξ). If M is invertible, then
G(x,ξ)=G0​(x,ξ)−∑j=1n​hj​(x)[M−1b(ξ)]j​.
(6)
The added terms are homogeneous solutions, so the Dirac delta source is preserved. Applying the boundary operators gives b−MM−1b=0. Any two such Green functions differ, for fixed source position, by a homogeneous solution with coefficient vector in the null space of M; invertibility therefore proves uniqueness. A singular boundary matrix signals a nontrivial homogeneous solution satisfying the endpoint conditions, where a compatibility condition and a nonunique inverse may arise. For L=D2, one convenient fundamental solution is (x−ξ)H(x−ξ).

Time support from poles of a Fourier Green function

Words: 49
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For the inverse transform G(τ)=∫dωe−iωτg(ω)/(2π), positive τ requires closing a decaying contour below the real axis, clockwise; negative τ requires closing above, counterclockwise. Poles strictly below give a retarded Green function, while poles strictly above give an advanced Green function. Real-axis poles need a prescription. The sign convention in the Fourier exponential is essential.

Fourier Green function in a spatially varying background

Words: 79
Green's function OurBigBook.com
A static background permits a Fourier transform of time difference, but a spatially varying coefficient generally prevents dependence on position difference alone. A momentum-space Green function then carries an incoming and an outgoing momentum, or equivalently one momentum together with the source position. Multiplication by a background field becomes a convolution, with a source-position phase when the Fourier basis is written as eik⋅(r−r′). A diagonal single-momentum representation is justified only with additional spatial translation symmetry or an explicitly fixed source origin.

Advanced Green function (GA​(t,t′)=0(t>t′))

Words: 59
Green's function OurBigBook.com
An advanced Green function has support only before its source time. It is selected by a future boundary condition, rather than an initial causal response. For L=∂t2​+2λ∂t​+ω02​ with λ<0 and Ω2=ω02​−λ2>0, the real-axis inverse Fourier transform of (−ω2−2iλω+ω02​)−1 is −H(−t)e−λtsin(Ωt)/Ω. Its first derivative jumps by one at zero. A growing retarded solution exists with a different inverse contour; this illustrates causality versus stability of a Green function.

Source-position-dependent Fourier Green function (Gr′​(k;ω))

Words: 70
Green's function OurBigBook.com
A static but spatially inhomogeneous linear operator has time translation symmetry without spatial translation symmetry. At fixed source position r′, one may still Fourier transform its Green function in x=r−r′. The coefficient retains r′ as a parameter. A multiplication by V(r) becomes a convolution with Vr′​(q)=eiq⋅r′V(q), not a spatially diagonal multiplier unless V is constant. Suppressing the source-position subscript is only a notational convention.

Neumann Green function with constant boundary flux (Δx​G(x,x0​)=δ(x−x0​),∂n​G=1/∣S∣)

Words: 97
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For a smooth bounded connected domain V with boundary S, integrating the Green function equation and applying the divergence theorem forces ∫S​∂n​GdS=1. Thus zero Neumann boundary data are incompatible with an unmodified unit point source. The displayed constant boundary derivative has the required total flux. For ΔΦ=σ and ∂n​Φ=f, the compatibility condition is ∫V​σdV=∫S​fdS. Green's second identity then yields
Φ(x0​)=∫V​G(x,x0​)σ(x)dV−∫S​G(x,x0​)f(x)dS+∣S∣1​∫S​ΦdS.
(7)
The last term is an undetermined additive constant. Adding a constant to G does not change the other two terms together, because of the compatibility condition. This construction keeps the unit Dirac delta source; using a mean-subtracted source with zero normal derivative is a different normalization.

Half-line Green function for the first cylindrical harmonic (G(x,s)=−2s​max(x,s)min(x,s)​)

Green's function OurBigBook.com
For Ly=y′′+y′/x−y/x2 on x>0, impose y(0)=0 by a continuous limit and y(x)→0 at infinity. The adapted homogeneous solutions are x at zero and 1/x at infinity, with Wronskian −2/x. The displayed Green function is continuous and its first derivative has jump one at x=s, so Lx​G(x,s)=δ(x−s) with ordinary source measure ds. For continuous f with ∫0∞​(1+s2)∣f(s)∣ds<∞,
y(x)=∫0∞​G(x,s)f(s)ds=−2x1​∫0x​s2f(s)ds−2x​∫x∞​f(s)ds.
(8)
This solves Ly=f with the stated endpoint limits. No nonzero combination of x,1/x meets both homogeneous endpoint conditions, proving uniqueness. Multiplying L by x gives the self-adjoint expression (xy′)′−y/x, explaining the weighted reciprocity xG(x,s)=sG(s,x).

Bounded Green kernel for a radial Euler operator (G(x,s)=−min(x,s)/(3max(x,s)2))

Words: 110
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For Ly=(x2y′)′−2y on x>0, choose solutions bounded at zero and infinity. The homogeneous Cauchy-Euler equation has basis x,x−2. Joining the left-regular and right-regular solutions continuously and imposing s2[Gx​]s−s+​=1 gives the displayed Green's function with ordinary integration measure ds. For bounded forcing,
y(x)=−3x21​∫0x​sf(s)ds−3x​∫x∞​s2f(s)​ds.
(9)
The integrals converge and give the unique bounded solution: no nonzero homogeneous combination is bounded at both ends. If 0≤f≤M, negativity of the kernel gives −M/2≤y≤0. Differentiation cancels the two moving-endpoint terms, leaving
y′(x)=3x32​∫0x​sf(s)ds−31​∫x∞​s2f(s)​ds,
(10)
which implies ∣y′(x)∣≤M/(3x). For constant forcing f=M, the bounded solution is −M/2; the endpoint conditions are boundedness, rather than zero endpoint values.

Green function of an undamped oscillator (L=∂x2​+k2)

Words: 86
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For zero initial value and slope, the causal Green function is G0​(x,s)=H(x−s)sin[k(x−s)]/k, with k=0 and H the Heaviside step function. For zero values at endpoints a<b, put κ=∣k∣. The Dirichlet Green function is
GD​(x,s)=−κsin[κ(b−a)]sin[κ(x<​−a)]sin[κ(b−x>​)]​.
(11)
Both are continuous at the source and have a first-derivative jump of one, giving Lx​G=δ(x−s). The Dirichlet inverse exists when sin[κ(b−a)]=0; a zero denominator signals a nontrivial homogeneous mode and a Fredholm solvability condition. The endpoint kernel is the zero-conjugation case of the Dirichlet Green function for a conjugated harmonic oscillator. Boundary conditions determine which kernel must be integrated against a forcing term.

Green kernels for a radial dipole Euler equation (L=∂x2​+x−1∂x​−x−2)

Words: 130
Green's function OurBigBook.com
The homogeneous Cauchy-Euler equation Ly=0 has fundamental solutions x,x−1 on x>0, with Wronskian −2/x. Requiring decay at both endpoints gives the unweighted Green's function
GD​(x,ξ)={−x/2,−ξ2/(2x),​x≤ξ,x≥ξ.​
(12)
Requiring zero initial value and derivative at zero instead gives the forward kernel
G0​(x,ξ)={0,(x−ξ2/x)/2,​x≤ξ,x≥ξ.​
(13)
Both kernels are continuous and have first-derivative jump one at x=ξ, so Lx​G=δ(x−ξ). Away from that point they solve the homogeneous equation. Integrating against the forcing with ordinary measure dξ yields the respective solutions whenever the integral and endpoint limits converge. Their difference is G0​−GD​=x/2, independent of ξ, so the solutions differ by the homogeneous term (x/2)∫f(ξ)dξ for integrable forcing. For example, the two choices for an indicator forcing on (0,1) differ by x/2. Specifying a differential operator without its endpoint conditions does not specify its Green kernel.

Green kernel and endpoint compatibility for a singular Euler equation (Lu=x2u′′+xu′−u)

Words: 139
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For 0<x<1, the homogeneous Cauchy-Euler equation has solutions x,x−1. The left-vanishing solution x and right-vanishing solution x−x−1 give the unweighted Green function G(x,s)=x(1−s−2)/2 for x≤s and (x−x−1)/2 for x≥s. It is continuous at x=s and its first derivative has jump 1/s2, so Lx​G=δ(x−s).
For continuous forcing f on [0,1], its integral is
u(x)=2x−x−1​∫0x​f(s)ds+2x​∫x1​(1−s−2)f(s)ds.
(14)
This is bounded at zero and vanishes at one, but u(0+)=−f(0). The first singular term uses the average x−1∫0x​f→f(0). In the other, the substitution t=x/s gives x∫x1​f(s)s−2ds=∫x1​f(x/t)dt→f(0) by dominated convergence. Thus the two zero endpoint values require f(0)=0. When compatible, the solution is unique among bounded solutions because no nonzero combination of x,x−1 meets both homogeneous endpoint conditions. This example shows why pointwise endpoint behavior of a Green function does not itself justify passing a limit through its integral.

The adapted solutions are sinhx/x at zero and e−x/x at infinity, with Wronskian −x−2. Green kernel with a vanishing Wronskian at an interior singular point (G(x,ξ)=u(min(x,ξ))v(max(x,ξ))/W(ξ))

Words: 133
Green's function OurBigBook.com
The usual Green function formula for a monic second-order equation requires a nonzero Wronskian at the source. At an interior singular point it may fail to define an ordinary inverse for arbitrary forcing. For example, for Ly=y′′−(1+x)y′/x+y/x on [−1,1], choose u=1+x and v=ex−e(1+x)/2. They satisfy the left and right Dirichlet boundary conditions, and W=uv′−u′v=xex. The displayed kernel is valid for ξ=0 and has unit jump in its first x derivative. Its 1/ξ behaviour prevents unrestricted integration through zero. For smooth forcing f(x)=xq(x), the product G(x,ξ)f(ξ) has a removable singularity, and its integral gives the unique solution extending with two continuous derivatives through zero. That matching condition matters: merely requiring one continuous derivative allows additional piecewise homogeneous solutions. A smooth forcing with f(0)=0 cannot have a solution with two continuous derivatives there, as expansion of xy′′−(1+x)y′+y=xf shows.

Decaying two-sided Green function of a constant-coefficient ordinary differential equation

Words: 135
Green's function OurBigBook.com
Let p(D) be a constant-coefficient differential operator, D=d/dt, with distinct characteristic roots λj​ having nonzero real parts. The solution of p(D)K=δ decaying at both temporal infinities is
K(t)=H(t)∑Reλj​<0​p′(λj​)eλj​t​−H(−t)∑Reλj​>0​p′(λj​)eλj​t​,
(15)
where H is the Heaviside step function. This follows by partial fraction decomposition of 1/p(z) and the first-order kernels eλtH(t) for Reλ<0, or −eλtH(−t) for Reλ>0. Both first-order kernels jump by one and solve (D−λ)Kλ​=δ as distributions.
For example, p(D)=(D+1)(D−2)(D+2) gives
K(t)={−e2t/12,−e−t/3+e−2t/4,​t<0,t>0.​
(16)
It is continuous together with its first derivative; its second derivative jumps by one, as required by the jump conditions for a third-order Green function. A solution of p(D)y=f is the convolution K∗f when it exists. If positive-real-part roots occur, decay at both ends generally requires a nonzero negative-time branch: this is the distinction captured by causality versus stability of a Green function. A causal kernel would retain growing positive-time terms and need not have a real-axis Fourier transform.

Nonunique Green kernel at a singular endpoint with two vanishing modes (Ly=y′′−3y′/x+3y/x2)

Words: 111
Green's function OurBigBook.com
On 0<x<1, both independent homogeneous solutions x,x3 vanish at the singular endpoint zero. Consequently imposing y(0)=y(1)=0 leaves the nonzero homogeneous solution x3−x and does not determine a unique inverse. One valid right Green function, with Lx​G=δ(x−z) and zero endpoint values, is
G0​(x,z)={x(z3−z)/(2z3),(x3−x)/(2z2),​x≤z,x≥z.​
(17)
Its first derivative has jump one because the Wronskian of x and x3−x is 2z3. Every kernel G0​+(x3−x)h(z) preserves these properties when the integrals exist. For sources supported away from zero, integration yields one particular solution; the full endpoint-constrained family adds C(x3−x). An additional endpoint selection, such as y(x)/x→0, can choose a unique member. This is a singular-endpoint phenomenon, not an ordinary regular two-point uniqueness theorem.

Words: 63
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For 0<a<b, the displayed decaying Green function solves (−∂x2​+a2)(−∂x2​+b2)K=δ0​ on the real line. Its Fourier transform is
K(k)=(k2+a2)(k2+b2)1​=b2−a21​(k2+a21​−k2+b21​).
(18)
Invert each term using the one-dimensional modified Helmholtz Green function. Then a decaying solution with forcing h is the convolution K∗h. For a=1,b=2, this gives K=e−∣x∣/6−e−2∣x∣/12 for the operator ∂x4​−5∂x2​+4. Its first-derivative jump cancels, while its third-derivative jump is one, providing the unit Dirac delta distribution required by the fourth-order operator.

Causal Green function for a repeated-root Euler operator (G(x,ξ)=H(x−ξ)xrξ1−rlog(x/ξ),r=(1−α)/2)

Words: 123
Green's function OurBigBook.com
For L=y′′+αy′/x+(α−1)2y/(4x2) on x>0, the repeated indicial root is r=(1−α)/2 and the homogeneous solutions are xr,xrlogx. Their Wronskian is x−α. The displayed causal Green function is continuous at each source ξ>0, has a unit jump in its first derivative, and satisfies Lx​G=δ(x−ξ). It is zero near the origin, so its value and first derivative there vanish. Those origin conditions alone fail to give uniqueness when α<−1: then both homogeneous solutions and their first derivatives vanish as x↓0. For forcing f(x)=x, source integration from zero converges when α>−5 and gives yp​=4x3/(α+5)2. All zero-origin-data solutions in −5<α<−1 are yp​+xr(C1​+C2​logx); for α≥−1 the solution is unique. Causality selects the displayed kernel even when the bare singular-endpoint conditions are insufficient.

Integration against a compactly supported forcing gives the unique solution decaying at both boundaries.

Dipole Green tensor angular cancellation (K=3bI​δ−pv4πbr33n⊗n−I​)

Green's function OurBigBook.com
For the three-dimensional reference Green function g(r)=1/(4πbr), the distributional mixed Hessian K=∇x​∇x′​g has the displayed contact and principal-value parts. Since the spherical mean of n⊗n is I/3, its ordinary dipole part has zero angular integral. Radial weighting therefore isolates the contact term, provided boundary truncation is absent or negligible in the bulk limit.

Green's function OurBigBook.com
The impulse response records the response to a unit impulse, with specified initial or boundary conditions. In continuous time the impulse is a Dirac delta function; in discrete time it is the Kronecker delta δ[n]. For a linear time-invariant system with zero initial state, the response to a general input is its convolution with the impulse response. The impulse response of a causal filter is zero before the impulse.
For the five-sample moving average, a discrete impulse produces h[n]=1/5 at n=0,1,2,3,4 and zero otherwise. The response lasts five samples, so this is a finite impulse response system. Its frequency response is the finite sum of the five delayed phase contributions: one short input experiment determines how every sustained sinusoid is filtered.
